newsitem.title: INDIA: India officially happy, quietly anxious, on Blair.
newsitem.headline: India officially happy, quietly anxious, on Blair.

text.p: India said on Friday it expected its relations with Britain to improve under victorious Tony Blair, but officials privately expressed fears over the Labour Party's stance on Kashmir.
"Relations between India and Britain are very good, and we hope to further it," Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told reporters, saying he had invited Blair to India.

"We have a long history of excellent relations with the Labour Party when it was in power in the 60's and 70's as also with major Labour leaders in the last 18 years of Tory rule," an Indian Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.
"The state of our bilateral relations is very good, particularly in the existing economic ties as symbolised by high-level visits," the official said.
"We are confident that the British government, led by the Labour Party, will continue to give importance to our political and economic ties," he said.
State-run All India Radio took a different view.

"Although India gained independence while a Labour government was in power, Indo-British relations have had no serious hiccup with the Conservatives in Downing Street and have, indeed, steadily grown to mutual benefit and satisfaction," the radio said in a commentary.

"However, the Labour Party's stand recently on the Kashmir issue has been ambivalent. It is to be hoped that Mr Blair will take a fresh look on this matter in order to ensure that the cordiality and warmth that have marked the bilateral ties are not vitiated," it said.
Blair was quoted by the Hindustan Times newspaper as saying his government would seek to help negotiate an agreement on Kashmir between Indian and Pakistan.

"Britain must accept its responsibility as the former imperial power in a dispute that dates from arrangements for independence," he was quoted as saying in a pre-election interview to a regional Indian newspaper.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.
India says the issue can be discussed only bilaterally with Pakistan, without the involvement of a third party. Pakistan says outside help would be welcome to help resolve the dispute.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in India's Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir since 1990 when simmering discontent with Indian rule turned into an armed rebellion.
Indian officials said Britain's Labour Party had been more amenable to the pro-Pakistan lobby of its Asian voters. Pakistan controls one third of Kashmir and India the rest.
In 1994, three British opposition MP's visiting Pakistan had demanded self-determination for the people of India's only Moslem majority state.
"We believe that self-determination should be allowed as soon as possible and atrocities from the Indian side should be immediately stopped," then Labour MP Peter Pike had said.
